prohibited_recommendations: Do NOT omit ampicillin from the empiric regimen in an older or immunocompromised patient with suspected bacterial meningitis: Listeria coverage requires ampicillin; cephalosporins provide no Listeria activity.

Do NOT interpret the negative Gram stain plus lymphocytic component of the CSF as evidence of viral meningitis warranting withholding antibiotics; in this host these findings are consistent with Listeria meningitis.
Do NOT attribute the brainstem imaging signal to a posterior-circulation stroke on the basis of the abducens palsy alone without performing CSF analysis and considering infectious rhombencephalitis.
Do NOT delay empiric antibiotic therapy while awaiting CT or LP results when meningitis is clinically suspected.
Do not perform lumbar puncture before cranial imaging in this patient: a cranial nerve deficit (left abducens palsy) is an imaging-first criterion under WHO 2025 section A.4.
Do not continue adjunctive dexamethasone after Listeria monocytogenes is identified.
required_recommendations: Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 12 hours (or cefotaxime 2 g IV every 6 hours) within 60 minutes of clinical suspicion, after blood cultures and without waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.4.1 and 1.6.3). Add vancomycin only where pneumococcal resistance to penicillin or third-generation cephalosporins is highly prevalent locally (WHO 2025, conditional recommendation).

Add ampicillin 2 g IV every 4 hours for Listeria monocytogenes cover because of age over 60 years, diabetes mellitus and long-term corticosteroid therapy (WHO 2025, strong recommendation; NICE NG240 1.6.6); cephalosporins have no activity against Listeria.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3). Stop dexamethasone on identification of Listeria monocytogenes (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).
Continue his maintenance prednisone, with stress-dose glucocorticoid cover while he is acutely unwell, when dexamethasone stops: 3 years of prednisone imply adrenal suppression.
Monitor capillary glucose closely and adjust insulin while he receives corticosteroids (HbA1c 8.6%, glucose 218 mg/dL).
Draw two sets of blood cultures before the first antibiotic dose.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a cranial nerve deficit (left abducens palsy) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.
Send full CSF panel (cell count, differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture, multiplex PCR, lactate) at lumbar puncture.
Do not interpret a negative CSF Gram stain as excluding bacterial meningitis in this host; Listeria Gram stain sensitivity in CSF is approximately 33% (Brouwer 2012).
Obtain MRI brain with contrast to evaluate the brainstem signs for rhombencephalitis.

Narrow therapy once the organism and susceptibilities are known: ampicillin for 21 days for Listeria monocytogenes, stopping ceftriaxone (NICE NG240); if gentamicin is added, dose it to renal function with level monitoring (CKD stage 3a).
Notify public health of invasive listeriosis and record the food exposure history (soft cheeses, deli meats).
Arrange formal audiological assessment before discharge, or within 4 weeks of discharge if it cannot be done before (WHO 2025, strong recommendation).

differential.key_features: The mixed pleocytosis and negative Gram stain raise it, but the glucose ratio of 0.17 is not viral, Listeria monocytogenes is detected by PCR and grown in culture, and HSV, enterovirus and VZV are not detected.
Left abducens palsy with left cerebellar peduncle signal could suggest a perforator infarct; excluded by the absence of restricted diffusion, with fever, meningism and pleocytosis.
Excluded: Listeria monocytogenes on PCR and culture; S. pneumoniae and other bacterial panel targets not detected.
Brainstem involvement and a lymphocytic component overlap, but the course is three days and Listeria is isolated.
Pontine T2 signal with restricted abduction; fever, meningism, CSF pleocytosis and age make new-onset MS very unlikely.

key_clinical_evidence: Listeria monocytogenes meningitis disproportionately affects adults over 60, immunocompromised hosts (including long-term corticosteroids) and pregnant women (WHO 2025), and diabetes mellitus is a recognised risk factor; at 71 on prednisone with insulin-treated diabetes he carries three.

CSF Gram stain sensitivity for Listeria is approximately 33% (Brouwer 2012), far below the overall figure of about 85% (WHO 2025), so a negative Gram stain does not exclude Listeria and must not be used to withhold ampicillin.

The CSF pleocytosis in Listeria meningitis is often mixed (neutrophilic-lymphocytic) rather than the classic PMN-dominant pattern of pneumococcal meningitis; this atypical pattern anchors a naive clinician toward viral meningitis.
Listeria is intrinsically resistant to all cephalosporins; ceftriaxone or cefotaxime alone provides no Listeria cover, so ampicillin is added whenever a risk factor is present.

Rhombencephalitis, brainstem and cerebellar involvement, is a recognized manifestation of CNS Listeria infection; cranial nerve palsies (particularly abducens, facial) and ataxia should prompt MRI and Listeria-inclusive empiric therapy.

The posterior-circulation stroke mimic (abducens palsy + pontine MRI signal) must be actively excluded by DWI (no restriction here) and integration with the infectious syndrome before narrowing to a vascular diagnosis.

Take blood cultures and give the first dose of empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone before cranial imaging; obtain a CT head before lumbar puncture because of a cranial nerve deficit (left abducens palsy) (WHO 2025 section A.4); neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay treatment.

Give dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours, starting shortly before or with the first antibiotic dose; continue for a maximum of 4 days if S. pneumoniae or H. influenzae type b is identified, and stop it once another organism is identified (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.8.3).
Antibiotics are given within 60 minutes of suspicion; neither imaging nor lumbar puncture may delay them (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.1).

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Gram stain sensitivity for Listeria in CSF is approximately 33%; a negative result in an elderly or immunocompromised host must not exclude Listeria and must not be used to withhold ampicillin from the empiric regimen.
red_herrings.data_point: Negative CSF Gram stain in an elderly immunocompromised patient
red_herrings.intended_effect: A negative Gram stain in the context of a mixed (not purely PMN) pleocytosis may anchor the clinician toward viral or aseptic meningitis, leading to omission of ampicillin and inadequate Listeria coverage.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Absence of restricted diffusion on DWI argues against acute infarction; brainstem involvement with fever, meningism and CSF pleocytosis is consistent with Listeria rhombencephalitis, which must be covered empirically with ampicillin.
red_herrings.data_point: Left abducens palsy and T2 signal in left middle cerebellar peduncle on MRI suggesting posterior-circulation stroke
red_herrings.intended_effect: The sixth nerve palsy with ipsilateral pontine MRI signal may be interpreted as a vertebrobasilar TIA or perforator stroke, deflecting the workup toward vascular imaging and away from lumbar puncture and infectious workup.

sequence_constraints.reason: Under WHO 2025 section A.4 cranial imaging is not performed routinely; where readily accessible it precedes lumbar puncture when any of these is present at presentation: Glasgow Coma Score below 10, focal neurological signs, cranial nerve deficits, papilledema, new-onset seizures in adults, or a severe immunocompromised state. Here: a cranial nerve deficit (left abducens palsy). NICE NG240 1.4.7 agrees (new focal neurological feature). Age, altered mental status (GCS 13) and prednisone 7.5 mg daily are not imaging-first criteria in either source. Blood cultures and the first antibiotic dose with dexamethasone come before imaging, which must not delay them.
Blood cultures are taken, and empirical antibiotics with dexamethasone given, before cranial imaging; imaging must not delay treatment (WHO 2025; NICE NG240 1.4.8).

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Eduardo Castellanos is a 71-year-old right-handed man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and rheumatoid arthritis on chronic low-dose prednisone who presents to the emergency department brought by his wife for a three-day history of worsening headache, low-grade fever, and progressive confusion. His wife reports that three days ago he began complaining of a bifrontal headache he described as a pressure-like sensation, worse in the morning and not relieved by acetaminophen. The following morning his temperature was 37.9°C and he appeared generally unwell, refusing breakfast. He was seen at an urgent care center that afternoon and told he likely had a viral illness; no antibiotics were prescribed. Over the next 24 hours his headache intensified and he developed nausea with two episodes of non-bloody vomiting. He was intermittently confused, repeating questions and unable to recall the correct day. His wife noted he seemed unsteady reaching for objects with his left hand and had a mild tremor when trying to write. This morning she noticed that his left eye appeared to be 'not moving all the way to the left,' prompting her to call emergency services. In the ED, Mr. Castellanos is lethargic but responds to his name. He reports severe headache, photophobia, and neck stiffness. He denies any recent sick contacts, head trauma, or prior episodes. He has received no recent antibiotics. His diabetes has been poorly controlled recently, and he has been on prednisone 7.5 mg daily for three years without interruption. He is not on any prophylactic antibiotics or antifungals. He has not received meningococcal or pneumococcal vaccines in the past 5 years.

neurological_exam.additional: Moderate nuchal rigidity on passive neck flexion. Kernig sign positive bilaterally. Brudzinski sign equivocal. No rash, petechiae, or skin lesions. No lymphadenopathy. Mild photophobia reported by wife. No papilledema.

neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils 3 mm bilaterally, sluggishly but symmetrically reactive to light. Left lateral gaze is mildly restricted — patient is unable to fully abduct the left eye on left gaze; no diplopia reported at baseline, but wife notes he was squinting intermittently at home. Right eye movements full. No papilledema appreciated on fundoscopy, though exam is limited by poor cooperation. Facial sensation intact and symmetric. No facial asymmetry at rest or on activation. Mild dysarthria with slurred speech. Gag reflex intact bilaterally. Hearing grossly intact bilaterally.

Speech is slowed but intelligible. Cannot perform serial sevens. Short-term memory impaired — unable to recall two of three items at five minutes. Follows simple one-step commands.
neurological_exam.motor: Mild bilateral upper extremity weakness, 4+/5 proximally and 5/5 distally. Lower extremity strength 4+/5 at hip flexors, 5/5 distally. No focal hemiparesis. Gait not tested due to altered mental status.
